extracted.intended_audience: general readers, historians, students, and scholars researching Martin Luther King Jr.'s authorship and alleged plagiarism
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate authorship and plagiarism issues in Martin Luther King Jr.'s academic papers and speeches, including documentary evidence, institutional investigations, and scholarly interpretations. The page presents factual findings, examples, and competing scholarly views about attribution, citation practice, and rhetorical traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual appropriation in doctoral dissertation
rubrics_metrics.description: King's doctoral dissertation included large sections from a dissertation written by another student (Jack Boozer) three years earlier at Boston University.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: large verbatim or near-verbatim passages taken from another student's work. Evaluation focuses on extent and verbatim overlap between King's dissertation and earlier student work; detection typically requires side-by-side comparison of texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation and plagiarism of major portions
rubrics_metrics.description: Boston University conducted an investigation that found he appropriated and plagiarized major portions of his doctoral thesis from various other authors who wrote about the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional findings classify copying as 'appropriation'/'plagiarism' when significant portions derive from other authors without proper attribution. Guidance includes relying on university committee review procedures and documented source comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper citation practices / use of quotations and footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: King had faulty citation practices: numerous passages were included without appropriate quotations and citations of sources, and reviewers noted a lack of extensive footnotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete indicators: missing quotation marks for quoted material, failure to record proper source citations, and insufficient footnoting. University practice attaches notes to theses where citations are missing; good practice requires explicit quotations and full citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notetaking practices as root cause
rubrics_metrics.description: King's faulty citation practices were rooted in the notecards he created while conducting research; large sections of chapters are verbatim transcriptions of these notecards in which errors were perpetuated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should consider research workflows: whether notes recorded sources correctly, whether verbatim notecard text was later incorporated without quotes, and whether systematic notetaking failures led to unacknowledged borrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern of borrowing across career (papers, sermons, speeches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances of textual appropriation appear in King's earliest extant writings as well as his dissertation; the pattern is also noticeable in his speeches and sermons throughout his career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should look beyond single incidents to patterns across multiple works. Repeated un-attributed borrowing across genres strengthens the case for problematic practice rather than isolated error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing scholarly plagiarism from preaching traditions (voice merging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some scholars argue that 'voice merging' — using the words of scripture, sacred text, and prior preachers — follows a long tradition of preaching and should not be termed plagiarism; others view such borrowing as imitation or plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation must account for genre/context: in sermons and oratory, reuse of traditional phrases may be accepted or praised, whereas in academic writing strict citation norms apply. Analysts should explicitly state the normative standard used (academic vs. homiletic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of intent and culpability
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars and the Boston University panel wrestled with whether King's actions were unintentional (e.g., sloppy notetaking, busy pastoral life) or deliberate; Clayborne Carson thought King acted unintentionally, though he also noted King was familiar enough with academic norms to know better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations of intent influence judgments and sanctions. Evidence relevant to intent includes writing habits, notecard practices, prior training in citation, contemporaneous comments by advisors, and whether similar borrowing recurs after training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty review and detection standards
rubrics_metrics.description: King's readers (faculty reviewers) failed to notice problematic use of sources; some reviewers saw issues but dismissed them as anomalous and still praised the dissertation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of oversight should consider reviewers' expertise, thoroughness of review, and institutional standards at the time. Failure to detect problems does not negate the existence of problematic borrowing but may explain historical non-action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional response and remedy criteria (revocation vs notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boston University decided not to revoke his doctorate, saying that although King acted improperly, his dissertation still 'makes an intelligent contribution to scholarship.' A letter was attached to the dissertation noting passages without appropriate quotations and citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions balance severity of misconduct against the substantive contribution of the work when choosing remedies. Possible actions include attaching corrective notes, censure, or degree revocation; guidance: document the rationale and proportionality of the remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of secondary sources and adequacy of paraphrase
rubrics_metrics.description: King's paper 'The Chief Characteristics and Doctrines of Mahayana Buddhism' was taken almost entirely from secondary sources, raising concerns about adequacy of paraphrase and original contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether text is original synthesis or an aggregation of secondary sources without proper transformation or attribution. Indicators of inadequate paraphrase include close structural correspondence, similar phrasing, and lack of citation to secondary works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity in speeches to prior speakers and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of speeches (for example the closing of 'I Have a Dream') resemble earlier addresses and phrases (e.g., Prathia Hall's 'I have a dream' phrase and Archibald Carey Jr.'s 1952 address).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating speech authorship, consider oral tradition, shared rhetorical repertoire, direct influence, and whether verbal borrowings were acknowledged or part of accepted rhetorical practice. Use historical documentation (correspondence, contemporaneous accounts) to trace sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly disagreement and interpretive framing
rubrics_metrics.description: There is scholarly debate: some view King's borrowing as plagiarism; others interpret it as imitation, transformation, or a preacherly practice; various journal articles and books present competing analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should cite and weigh multiple scholarly positions, explain analytical frameworks (legal/academic vs. rhetorical/historical), and be explicit about which standards of authorship and originality they apply when drawing conclusions.
